extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) including rebuttal evidence (teaching away, unexpected results, result-effective variables), and special rules when a prior art genus encompasses a claimed species. Directed to examination of patentability under MPEP case law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in proportions — criticality and difference in kind
rubrics_metrics.description: "While a change in the proportions of a combination shown to be old... such changes must be critical as compared with the proportions used in the prior processes, producing a difference in kind rather than degree."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: In re Lilienfeld, In re Wells; later decisions such as E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co. v. Synvina C.V. and UCB, Inc. v. Actavis Labs stress that a modification of a process parameter may be patentable if it produces a new and unexpected result different in kind and not merely in degree. See MPEP § 716.02–§ 716.02(g) for discussion of criticality and unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading authorities: U.S. v. Adams; Depuy Spine v. Medtronic; Allergan v. Sandoz (example where prior art taught minimizing BAK). But a purported "teaching away" must be sufficiently discouraging of the claimed route (see In re Geisler where the reference did not teach away). See MPEP § 2145 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-effective variable (not recognized in the prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may rebut an obviousness rejection based on optimization by showing the claimed variable was not recognized in the prior art to be a result-effective variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonie provides the archetype where the prior art was silent regarding a variable in a critical ratio; E.I. Dupont v. Synvina discusses the concept and its narrowness. The examiner should require applicants to articulate why the variable would not have been recognized in the prior art. Note: after KSR, a known result-effective variable is one motivation among others for experimentation, but not the only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art discloses variable in a very broad range
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art discloses the variable within a range that is so broad, in light of dissimilar characteristics of the members, as to not invite optimization, that fact may weigh against an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Genetics Inst. v. Novartis where disclosure of 68,000 protein variants made ordinary motivation to optimize inapplicable. See MPEP §§ 2131.02, 2131.03, and 2144.08 for further guidance on range limitations and when a broad range undermines optimization-based obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining equivalents known for the same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is prima facie obvious to combine two compositions each of which is taught by the prior art to be useful for the same purpose... the idea of combining them flows logically from their having been individually taught in the prior art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative cases: In re Kerkhoven (spray-dried detergents), In re Crockett (treating cast iron), Ex parte Quadranti (mixture of known herbicides), In re Couvaras (combining known agents useful for same purpose). Use of this rationale supports a prima facie obviousness determination when both elements are taught for the same purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting equivalents known for the same purpose — art-recognized equivalency required
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on equivalency as a rationale supporting an obviousness rejection, the equivalency must be recognized in the prior art and cannot be based on applicant's disclosure or the mere fact that components are functional or mechanical equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: In re Ruff (Markush group alone insufficient), Smith v. Hayashi (evidence needed that alternatives were known photoconductors), In re Fout (express suggestion not necessary). Examiners should look for art-recognized equivalency evidence in the prior art itself rather than relying solely on applicant's disclosure or mere functional overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-recognized suitability for intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of a known material based on its suitability for its intended use can support a prima facie obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sinclair & Carroll v. Interchemical (printing ink solvent chosen for vapor pressure characteristics); additional examples: In re Leshin (selection of known plastic), Ryco v. Ag-Bag (hydraulic brakes known for same function in different environment). Examiners should identify prior art establishing suitable properties for the intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of species when prior art teaches a genus — single-reference approach
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species or subgenus but does not expressly disclose the particular claimed species, Office personnel should attempt to find additional prior art; absent that, consider specific factors to determine whether a single-reference 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor note: This MPEP section applies under AIA and pre-AIA regimes (timing differences noted). If additional art is not found, consider the list of detailed factors set out below (structure of genus, properties/utilities, predictability, number of species). See MPEP § 2144.08 and related subsections for full treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a prima facie case of obviousness — Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To make out a case of obviousness, Office personnel must (A) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluate any evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Graham v. John Deere; burden: PTO must establish prima facie case, then burden shifts to applicant to rebut. See related cases (In re Bell, Rijckaert, Oetiker) and MPEP §§ 714.12, 714.13, 715.09 for guidance on dealing with rebuttal evidence and when such evidence may be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: After construing the claims, Office personnel should determine the scope and content of the relevant prior art; each reference used must qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and be analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a prior art genus, make findings as to: (A) structure of disclosed genus and any expressly described species/subgenus; (B) physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed and any suggested limitations; (C) predictability of the technology; and (D) the number of species encompassed, considering all variables. See Panduit Corp. v. Dennison and MPEP § 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain differences between the closest disclosed prior art species and the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the closest disclosed prior art species or subgenus and compare it to the claimed species to determine similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities; evaluate whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities/differences; the inquiry is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex). Compare the claimed species to the closest prior art species of record and document structure, property, and utility differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the prior art from the perspective of a hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time; maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Ryko v. Nu-Star, Uniroyal v. Rudkin-Wiley. Typically, facts relevant to level of skill are in the prior art; however, consider any additional evidence presented by applicant. See MPEP §§ 2141 and 2141.03 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have had a reason to select the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the Graham findings and prior art teachings, determine whether it would have been obvious to select the claimed species/subgenus from the disclosed genus; consider specific indicia below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To address this issue, focus on all relevant prior art teachings and consider factors such as size of genus, express teachings recommending selection, and structural similarity to preferred species; account for number of variables to be selected/modified and the significance of differences between prior art and claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the size of the genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the size of the prior art genus, but recognize that size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; assess total circumstances (number of variations, alternatives, and the parent structural nucleus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small genus may sometimes anticipate a species (In re Petering), but a small number alone is not dispositive. Look to total circumstances including limited alternatives and little variation (Petering, Schaumann). See In re Ruschig for counterexamples where genus size did not support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider express teachings in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, point out that disclosure and explain why it would have made selection obvious to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Labs (express teaching to coadminister a named example), In re Kemps (one reference referring expressly to another). An express teaching may be an art-recognized equivalence or a specific disclosure that ties the references together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of structural similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a "typical," "preferred," or "optimum" species in the prior art is structurally similar to the claimed species, because structural similarity may provide a reason to select the claimed species based on expected similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Dillon, In re Deuel. Structural relationships (e.g., homologs, conservative amino acid substitutions) may motivate modification. But consider number of variables and significance of differences (In re Jones, In re Susi); in biotechnology conservative substitutions may be expected to have little effect, but context matters.
